definition.lead: Amazing Lab Experiments celebrates the experiments that make chemistry visible: colour changes, glowing reactions, oscillating clocks and classic demonstrations, with the chemistry behind each one.
definition.body: Behind every spectacular demonstration is a principle worth understanding: redox, catalysis, equilibrium, chemiluminescence. Many of these experiments are hazardous and must only be performed by trained people with proper safety equipment.

timeline.title: Oxygen
timeline.text: Joseph Priestley heats mercury oxide and collects a gas in which candles burn brightly.
timeline.why: A new element from a simple experiment.

timeline.title: What water is made of
timeline.text: Antoine Lavoisier shows that water forms from hydrogen and oxygen.
timeline.why: Water is a compound, not an element.

timeline.title: Splitting water with electricity
timeline.text: William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle electrolyse water.
timeline.why: Weeks after learning of Volta's new battery.

timeline.title: The iodine clock
timeline.text: Hans Landolt describes a reaction that turns blue-black suddenly after a delay.

timeline.title: Gold foil
timeline.text: Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden fire alpha particles at gold foil; a few bounce back.
timeline.why: Led Rutherford to the atomic nucleus.

timeline.title: Luminol
timeline.text: H. O. Albrecht describes the bright chemiluminescence of luminol.

timeline.title: An oscillating reaction
timeline.text: Boris Belousov observes a solution that changes colour back and forth.
timeline.why: At first, reviewers thought it impossible.

timeline.title: Life's building blocks in a flask
timeline.text: The Miller–Urey experiment makes amino acids from simple gases.

timeline.title: Briggs–Rauscher
timeline.text: Two teachers create a striking colour-oscillating reaction for classroom use.

quiz.q: Why does 'elephant toothpaste' foam so much?
options: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes quickly into oxygen gas, sped up by a catalyst
Soap reacts with air to release large amounts of nitrogen
Water boils instantly when it touches the soap mixture
Vinegar and baking soda release carbon dioxide inside
quiz.explain: Iodide or yeast catalase is the usual catalyst; soap traps the oxygen.

quiz.q: Why does the iodine clock turn blue-black suddenly?
options: Iodine builds up and binds starch once the thiosulfate is used up
A beam of light suddenly reaches the starch in the beaker
The solution cools below a critical temperature at once
Starch only turns blue once it has been fully dissolved
quiz.explain: The delay depends on concentrations and temperature.

quiz.q: Where does the light in a glow stick come from?
options: A chemical reaction that excites a dye: chemiluminescence
A tiny battery inside powers a light-emitting dye
A small amount of radioactive material excites the dye
Heat from mixing makes the liquid glow like a filament
quiz.explain: Breaking the inner vial mixes the reactants.

quiz.q: Why does luminol glow at crime scenes?
options: Iron in blood catalyses its oxidation
It reacts with water
It reacts with light only
It is radioactive
quiz.explain: It is a presumptive test, not proof.

options: Oscillates between colourless, amber and dark blue
Explodes once two clear solutions are mixed together
Freezes instantly, then melts back again in cycles
Glows green in the dark for several hours

quiz.q: At what temperature does liquid nitrogen boil?
options: About −196 °C
About 0 °C
About −78 °C
About −273 °C
quiz.explain: −78 °C is dry ice; −273 °C is absolute zero.

quiz.q: Why does a balloon shrink in liquid nitrogen?
options: The gas inside contracts as it cools (Charles's law)
The rubber melts
The air escapes
Nitrogen enters the balloon

quiz.q: Why does a lemon battery work?
options: Two different metals in an acidic electrolyte form a redox cell
Lemons store electricity collected from sunlight
Vitamin C molecules carry an electric charge by themselves
The citric acid makes the metals magnetic
quiz.explain: The lemon is just the electrolyte.

quiz.q: What did the gold foil experiment show?
options: Atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus
Atoms are solid
Gold is radioactive
Electrons orbit in circles
quiz.explain: Rutherford compared it to a shell bouncing off tissue paper.

quiz.q: Electrolysing water gives hydrogen and oxygen in a volume ratio of…
quiz.explain: H₂O has two hydrogens per oxygen.

quiz.q: The thermite reaction between iron oxide and aluminium is used to…
options: Weld railway tracks
Make ice
Purify water
Make glass
quiz.explain: It produces molten iron. Only for trained professionals.

quiz.q: Why must demonstrations like these be done by trained people?
options: Heat, toxic gases, splashes and explosions pose real risks
They are secret
They need expensive cameras
They only work in labs by law
quiz.explain: Safety glasses, gloves and planning are the minimum.
